lesson_title: The Magnet That Empties the Map
hook_text: Every January the buses leave the villages full of young people. Geography has a name for that — and a model.
clip_script: Scatter iron filings across a table with a magnet at the centre and watch them crawl inward. That is the whole core-periphery model in a single image. The magnet is the CORE — the region where the factories, banks, universities and ministries cluster. The table's edges are the PERIPHERY — the districts that send the core their minerals, their harvests and, most painfully, their children. Every new year, taxis and buses leave the villages of Limpopo and the old Transkei for Johannesburg, loaded with the young and the capable. That drain has a name: BACKWASH — the periphery's best, flowing coreward. And every arrival strengthens the magnet: more workers bring more shops, more taxes, better roads, and the better roads land the next factory. Success recruiting success — cumulative causation. Sometimes current flows outward instead: a mineworker's remittances raise a homestead roof; a firm opens a branch plant in a small town. Those trickles are SPREAD EFFECTS, and regional planning is honestly just plumbing — widen the spread pipes, narrow the backwash drain. And the move that scores: the picture repeats at every zoom. Rich North and supplying South. Gauteng magnet and homeland edges. Office-tower core and township rim, stitched together by one long taxi ride.
visual_style: Iron filings animating toward a glowing magnet over a map of South Africa; bus headlights streaming from village roads toward a city skyline; thin green arrows trickling back outward as a roof rises on a rural homestead; the same magnet pattern echoing at three zoom levels.
mood: Poignant but empowering — the model explains the ache and points at the fix.
pacing: Slow magnetic pull at the open, quickening as the magnet strengthens, three crisp zoom beats to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to run one model at three scales.
